candidate.answerReason: Triangle BCD is isosceles with vertex angle 120°, so its angle at D is 30°. Since rays DA and DC coincide, this is angle ADB.

methods.label: Method 1: Use an isosceles triangle
methods.explanation:
The equal radii give an isosceles triangle whose angle at \(D\) is the angle we want. Since \(ABC\) is equilateral, \(\angle ACB=60^\circ\). The points \(A,C,D\) lie on a line in that order, so
\[
\angle BCD=180^\circ-60^\circ=120^\circ.
\]
Both \(CB\) and \(CD\) are radii of the circle, so \(CB=CD=10\). Therefore triangle \(BCD\) has equal base angles, each measuring
\[
\frac{180^\circ-120^\circ}{2}=30^\circ.
\]
From \(D\), the rays \(DA\) and \(DC\) are the same ray. Hence \(\angle ADB=\angle CDB=30^\circ\), choice B.
methods.levelReason: Uses equal radii, equilateral and isosceles triangle angles, supplementary angles and the triangle angle sum.

methods.label: Method 2: Compare central and inscribed angles
methods.explanation:
Because \(ABC\) is equilateral, \(\angle ACB=60^\circ\). Since \(C\) is the circle's center, this is the central angle subtending the minor arc \(AB\).

The extension of \(AC\) through \(C\) places \(D\) opposite \(A\) on the circle, so \(D\) is outside the minor arc \(AB\). Thus the inscribed angle \(\angle ADB\) intercepts that minor arc. An inscribed angle is half the central angle intercepting the same arc, giving
\[
\angle ADB=\frac{60^\circ}{2}=30^\circ.
\]
The answer is \(30^\circ\), choice B.
methods.levelReason: Uses the standard school-geometry inscribed angle theorem and the 60° angles of an equilateral triangle.
